w: A working Dominican church deconsecrated after Napoleon, its vaulted Gothic nave now holds three storeys of books around a black steel bookcase built to hover clear of the frescoed walls. Browsers linger under stained glass with coffee from the altar-end cafe; voted the world's most beautiful bookshop in 2025 polls.
s: Bookshop inside a 13th-century Gothic church
why: Reader-voted world's most beautiful bookshop 2025, a genuine deconsecrated church

w: Opened in 1991 by Kunle Tejuosho as an offshoot of his mother's Glendora bookshop chain, this Awolowo Road shop stacks vinyl, secondhand books and African art under one roof, with a small cafe and live jazz evenings. Widely rated the best record collection on the continent, spanning highlife, Afrobeat, funk and juju.
s: Vinyl, books and jazz in a Lagos institution
why: West Africa's most storied record-and-book shop, running since 1991

w: James 'Jimmy' Rugami has sold secondhand vinyl from this cramped Kenyatta Market stall since 1989, after quitting DJing to chase records instead. Crates of benga, rumba, Congolese soukous and East African soul spill into the corridors, drawing crate-diggers and producers hunting rare 45s.
s: A crate-digger's stall deep in Kenyatta Market
why: A single crate-digger stall that became East Africa's vinyl mecca since 1989

w: Founded in 1974 and spread across an eight-storey former warehouse on Commissioner Street, this is reckoned the largest secondhand and rare bookshop in Africa, holding some two million books, maps, prints and old vinyl stacked to the ceiling in narrow, dimly lit aisles that feel more expedition than errand.
s: Africa's largest used bookshop, eight floors deep
why: Africa's largest used-book warehouse, two million items over eight floors

w: Mark Ernestus opened this shop in 1989 and it became the epicentre from which Berlin's techno and dub scene radiated, staffed by DJs who will play anything on request before you buy. It moved in 2023 after three decades on Paul-Lincke-Ufer, but the deep stock of house and techno twelve-inches remains unmatched.
s: Techno's ground-zero record shop since 1989
why: The record shop that shaped Berlin techno, running continuously since 1989

w: An escalator off Stortingsgata drops down to a sprawling basement of secondhand LPs, CDs, posters and film memorabilia, strong on punk and hardcore first pressings alongside Norwegian rock and jazz. Regulars call it a mythical vortex where time stops; it has been a fixture of Oslo's record-collecting scene for decades.
s: A basement of secondhand vinyl off Stortinget
why: Oslo's cult basement record shop, a fixture for generations of collectors

w: Around 250 dealers set up under the Tokyo International Forum's glass atrium on the first and third Sunday of each month, Japan's largest outdoor antique fair. Stalls run from Edo-period ceramics and vintage kimono to Showa-era toys, ukiyo-e prints and Western curios, drawing collectors before dawn.
s: Japan's biggest outdoor antique fair, twice a month
why: Japan's largest outdoor antique fair, running since the 1990s

w: Sprawling around Dongmyo Shrine, this market traces its trading roots to the Joseon dynasty and grew into its present antique-market form in the 1980s with some 600 stalls. Vintage clothing piled by the kilo, old vinyl, army surplus, cameras and curios spill across the pavement, popular with Seoul's thrifting youth.
s: Korea's biggest secondhand market, Joseon roots
why: Korea's biggest and oldest secondhand market, still ungentrified

w: A gilded gramophone hung above the door marks this stall on Saifee Jubilee Street inside Chor Bazaar, Mumbai's 150-year-old thieves' market. Stacks of old 78s and LPs in Hindi, English, Bengali and Telugu sit beside battered radios and wind-up phonographs the owner will crank up to demonstrate.
s: A golden gramophone marks Chor Bazaar's record stall
why: Chor Bazaar's landmark record-and-gramophone stall, marked by a golden phonograph

w: Booksellers have traded along the wall of Ezbekeya Garden since the 19th century, today some 132 stalls piled with secondhand paperbacks, out-of-print Arabic literature, vintage newspapers and old lithographs. Bargaining is expected; it remains downtown Cairo's essential haunt for readers on a budget.
s: 132 stalls of secondhand books against a garden wall
why: A 19th-century open-air book bazaar of 130-plus stalls, still trading

w: Antoine Naufal opened his first shop in 1933 opposite Beirut's Grand Theatre; the Hamra branch, trading since 1971, has outlasted civil war looting and repeated relocations of the flagship. Shelves run deep in Arabic, French and English titles, a touchstone of Beirut's literary life through decades of upheaval.
s: Lebanon's oldest bookshop chain, since 1933
why: Lebanon's oldest bookshop, trading through war and reconstruction since 1933

w: Since 2009 this Sunday-only market in Bomonti has drawn upward of 450 dealers selling typewriters, Ottoman coins, vintage clothing, old cameras and the odd piece of decommissioned US Army gear. Cash only and haggling expected, it is Istanbul's essential weekly rummage for collectors and thrifters.
s: 450 stalls of Istanbul bric-a-brac, every Sunday
why: Istanbul's biggest weekly antique bazaar, 450-plus stalls strong

w: Tucked behind an entrance off Kiraly utca in the old Jewish Quarter, this small shop stocks imported art, science and humanities titles bought directly from publishers worldwide, priced below what such rarities usually cost. It has run as both bookshop and small publishing house since the early 1990s.
s: An import bookshop hidden in a courtyard passage
why: A courtyard-hidden importer of rare foreign titles since the early 1990s

w: Set behind a heavy wrought-iron gate at the back of a courtyard off Wilcza street, this antiquarian bookshop requires visitors to ring the owner's bell to be let in. Inside, tightly packed shelves hold rare Polish first editions, prewar volumes and secondhand literature, a survivor of Warsaw's antiquarian trade.
s: Ring the bell for a hidden antiquarian bookshop
why: A bell-to-enter antiquarian bookshop tucked behind a courtyard gate

w: Its name means 'underground antiquarian,' and the shop lives up to it, tucked below street level on Hybernska opposite the side entrance of Masaryk railway station. Cramped shelves and stacked crates hold secondhand Czech and foreign titles, old maps and prints, a low-key survivor among Prague's antikvariats.
s: An underground antiquarian shop by Masaryk station
why: A literally underground secondhand bookshop by Prague's oldest station

w: Cris and Lucio Zaccara opened this as a vinyl record shop in 1982 before reinventing it as a bookshop, keeping a garden where readers linger and an upper floor for workshops, book clubs and live debates. A small in-house cafe serves coffee and cake; the record-shop roots still show in the music-book shelves.
s: A former vinyl shop turned garden bookstore
why: A 1982 vinyl shop reinvented as a garden-courtyard bookstore

w: Reckoned the largest record shop of its kind in Argentina, this San Telmo fixture on Defensa street stacks Argentine rock nacional, tango, cumbia and Latin folk alongside South American pressings of classic albums. Weekend crowds spill from the nearby antiques fair into its aisles, hunting rarities.
s: San Telmo's biggest crate-digging record shop
why: Argentina's biggest crate-digging record shop, on San Telmo's antiques strip

w: Yosef Halper opened this shop in 1990 in a narrow alley off Allenby Street, and it has grown into Israel's largest stock of used English-language books, over 60,000 titles strong with pockets of Judaica, militaria and rare science fiction. Maze-like aisles have drawn writers and browsers for three decades.
s: A maze of used English books off Allenby Street
why: Israel's largest secondhand English bookshop, running since 1990

w: Opened in 1998 on Skolavordustigur, this two-floor shop doubles as a record label with some 80 releases and became an informal clubhouse for Icelandic musicians including Bjork and Sigur Ros. Visitors can sit, sip free espresso and listen through the jazz-and-classical ground floor or indie-electronic basement.
s: The record shop Gramophone called the world's best
why: Gramophone magazine once called it the best record store in the world

w: Founded by a family of Jewish immigrants who fled Europe before the war, this bookshop on Avenida Jimenez has anchored Bogota's historic centre for decades, its towering shelves stocked with Colombian literature, imported titles and academic texts. It became a gathering point for writers and students through upheavals.
s: A colonial-era Bogota bookshop since the 1950s
why: A historic-centre bookshop run by the same family since the mid-20th century

w: Hidden inside a converted house on Calle San Francisco, this bookshop-cafe pairs curated fiction and design titles with a fern-filled terrace and a coffee bar, drawing Del Valle's readers to linger for hours. Opened in the 2020s but already feels like an institution, part literary salon, part quiet escape.
s: Books, coffee and ferns in a Del Valle courtyard
why: A converted-house bookshop-cafe that became Del Valle's literary living room

w: One of the world's largest weekend markets, Chatuchak packs some 15,000 stalls across 27 sections, with dedicated zones for secondhand clothing, vintage denim and antiques that supply resellers across Southeast Asia. Navigating its covered lanes in the heat is a rite of passage for collectors chasing rare finds.
s: 15,000 stalls, a vintage wing of its own
why: One of the world's largest weekend markets, with a serious vintage-clothing wing

w: Eslite pioneered the bookshop as round-the-clock cultural department store, mixing books with design retail, galleries and cafes; this branch inside the restored Songshan tobacco factory grounds took over as the chain's 24-hour flagship in 2024, a late-night refuge as much as a place to buy anything.
s: Taiwan's 24-hour bookshop-department-store hybrid
why: Taiwan's culture-defining 24-hour bookshop, now sited in an old tobacco factory

w: Run by radio personality Hiroshi Eguchi out of a converted residence in Harajuku's backstreets, this shop holds one of Japan's largest collections of independently published zines alongside art, design and fashion books. Warm wood shelving and soft light give it the feel of a friend's living room and cultural hub.
s: One of Japan's biggest zine collections, in a house
why: One of Japan's largest zine collections, in a converted Harajuku house

w: Former magazine editor Kim Hye-Mi and artist partner Yu Seong-Bo opened this Hongdae-area shop in 2014, filling it with art books, graphic novels and a deep run of vintage magazines alongside a children's section. Its curated, design-forward shelves are a fixture of Seoul's indie-publishing and zine-fair circuit.
s: Art books and vintage magazines near Hongdae
why: A curated art-book and vintage-magazine fixture of Seoul's indie scene since 2014

w: Spread outside the northern ramparts near the Bab El Khemis gate, one of Marrakech's oldest flea markets comes alive every Thursday with colonial Art Deco furniture, vintage mopeds, antique sewing machines, carved doors and stacks of old carpets. Bargaining is expected and the maze rewards unhurried wandering.
s: A Thursday flea market by Marrakech's old gate
why: One of Marrakech's oldest flea markets, a weekly sprawl by the city ramparts

w: Along a stretch of Hoang Hoa Tham street in Ba Dinh, a cluster of unmarked shops trade in antique pottery, porcelain, jade, bronzeware and old coins, largely unknown to tourists and favoured by Hanoi's own collectors. Prices and provenance both require negotiation, genuine antiques sitting shelf by shelf with fakes.
s: Hanoi's hidden antique row for old pottery and coins
why: Hanoi's low-key antique row, favoured by local collectors over tourists
